hooks.text: A missing hyphen did not actually destroy NASA's first interplanetary rocket.
Space history's most famous code error was not actually a missing hyphen.
An eighteen million dollar typo destroyed America's first probe to Venus.

title: The Missing Hyphen That Wasn't a Hyphen
description: NASA's Mariner 1 destroyed itself in 1962, but popular history got the coding glitch wrong.

beats.text: A missing hyphen did not actually destroy NASA's first interplanetary rocket.
beats.visual: Artist concept of the Mariner 1 probe near Venus, 1962

beats.text: On July 22, 1962, Mariner 1 launched toward Venus aboard an Atlas-Agena rocket.
beats.visual: Atlas-Agena rocket launching Mariner 1 from Cape Canaveral, 1962

beats.text: At 293 seconds, wild steering corrections forced a safety officer to detonate the spacecraft.
beats.visual: Photograph of Atlas-Agena rocket launch trajectory from Cape Canaveral, 1962

beats.text: Author Arthur C. Clarke and press accounts famously blamed a missing hyphen in guidance code.
beats.visual: Mainframe computer installation at Cape Canaveral tracking center, 1962

beats.text: In reality, programmers omitted a single mathematical overbar above the letter R in guidance equations.
beats.visual: Diagram of Mariner R spacecraft trajectory equations and guidance math, 1962

beats.text: Without that smoothing bar, the computer treated minor radar noise as violent velocity fluctuations.
beats.visual: Cape Canaveral Atlantic Missile Range tracking radar antenna, 1962

beats.text: That exact code had flown safely on lunar missions, but an in-flight hardware failure triggered the flaw.
beats.visual: Ranger lunar probe undergoing pre-flight testing at Jet Propulsion Laboratory, 1961

beats.text: Five weeks later Mariner 2 reached Venus, proving space history's most famous typo was not a hyphen.
beats.visual: Mariner 2 spacecraft in cleanroom with solar panels extended, 1962

better_than_last: Replaced the popular misnomer premise with the precise mathematical reality in the middle beats while maintaining a smooth loop back to the opening hook.
